provenance: Product documentation of the Industrial X-Ray prototype, condensed from README.md, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, docs/LIMITATIONS.md, docs/DATA_INTEGRATION.md and docs/SCENE_QUALITY.md. Describes how the prototype works; it is not plant data.

docs.title: What Industrial X-Ray is
docs.text: Industrial X-Ray is a browser pre-visit copilot for field technicians. It turns a 3D scan of an unfamiliar equipment room into a workspace: Explore the scan, Understand the cited diagnosis of an asset, Plan the maintenance with a virtual layout simulation, Practise on exploded teaching models (X-Ray, Learn, Practice), get remote Support from an expert, and see an illustrative Value calculator. The demo story follows a technician preparing to service pump P-005. It is decision support only: it reads data, highlights, plans and drafts; it has no connection to plant controls.

docs.title: The 3D scan and its integrity
docs.text: The 3D environment is a Gaussian-splat scan of an equipment room (Equipment Room.ply, 1,676,481 splats, all records valid). The browser renders 1,669,970 splats with view-dependent colour as compressed chunks; phones load the most important 730 thousand splats; a 2D floor plan replaces the 3D view when WebGL 2 is missing. The scan was rotated so the floor is level (RANSAC floor plane) and the walls are axis-aligned. Scale is treated as approximately metric (ceiling about 2.05 units) and was not surveyed. An earlier file, Industrial Boiler Room.ply, was corrupt from record 502,483 onward and is not used.

docs.title: How the objects in the scan were found and labelled
docs.text: Geometry first: splats with enough opacity are voxelised at 3 cm, floor, ceiling and four walls are fitted as planes, and the rest is clustered with DBSCAN into 676 object candidates, each with a gravity-aligned oriented 3D box. Then naming: a geometric/colour heuristic proposes a label, and a vision-language model (gpt-5.4-mini) looks at a context render and a close-up render of each box and picks one of 38 industrial classes with a confidence. When unsure it says 'other equipment' (260 objects) instead of guessing. 416 candidates have a specific type, 195 have confidence of at least 0.70, 7 labels were corrected in the team's AI-assisted visual review of renders (tagged review-corrected, not field-verified) and 30 are linked to workbook assets. Precision and recall have not been measured on a human-labelled sample; a check sheet is prepared for that.

docs.title: How workbook assets are linked to objects in the scan
docs.text: The 30 workbook assets have no real coordinates in the scan, so they are bound to compatible scan objects by a class-aware, one-to-one procedural mapping (for example a process pump to a pump-motor unit), preferring objects along the demo route; the target must be reachable by the robot. Every binding stores its method and a mapping confidence, which lowers the diagnosis confidence. On site, identity must be confirmed by tag, QR or NFC code before acting; a pilot would link assets through tags, QR/NFC codes or survey coordinates.

docs.title: How the inspection robot plans routes
docs.text: The robot is virtual. The floor is modelled as a height field on a 5 cm grid with several floor levels; obstacles are scan points between 0.12 m and 1.25 m above the local floor plus the footprints of extracted objects. A cell is walkable when it is observed floor and its distance-transform clearance is more than the 0.20 m robot radius. A* searches 8-connected cells with no corner cutting, a 0.18 m step limit and a cost that keeps the robot in the middle of aisles; line-of-sight smoothing shortens the path only inside walkable cells. An independent validation re-samples the route about every 2.5 cm and reports collisions (0) and minimum clearance. Block aisle adds an obstacle and re-plans from the robot's current position. Proximity: every asset within 1.2 m of the robot is framed and read out, forwards and in reverse. In the hosted demo the same planner runs in the browser as a JavaScript port.

docs.title: How the diagnosis and its confidence are produced
docs.text: An evidence engine (deterministic) gathers, for one asset: identity and current state, telemetry statistics comparing the last 12 hours with the asset's own first 24 hours and with class peers (z-scores), alarms matching the issue code or of high severity, work orders, historical service cases of the same class and issue, data-quality issues and documents. Hypotheses come from the equipment library and are linked to components; the leading hypothesis is shown with the alternatives. The workbook itself labels each asset's issue (for example FOULING for P-005 in Current_State); the copilot retrieves and explains the evidence for it, it does not discover the fault. Confidence is an evidence score, not a calibrated probability: model confidence x evidence support x (1 - data-quality penalty) x (0.6 + 0.4 x 3D mapping confidence); for P-005 it is 0.52. Maintenance priority = criticality weight x (100 - health) x model confidence, which makes P-005 the target. An LLM words the result following DOC-RAG-GUIDE and may cite only IDs from the evidence package; any other ID is removed by a citation checker. The checker verifies that each cited ID exists in the evidence, not that the sentence is fully supported by that record.

docs.title: What the copilot can do and how it stays grounded
docs.text: The 'Ask about the plant' copilot first applies transparent rules: find or locate objects in the scan, find the asset with an abnormal signal, find the faulty or highest-priority asset, open a diagnosis, send the robot, open the X-Ray view, Learn, Practice or the library. Other questions are answered from retrieved documents and the selected asset's evidence. With the backend running, a live LLM writes the answer and a checker removes citations that are not in the context. In the hosted (static) demo there is no live AI: answers are pre-generated by the same backend for common questions, or composed from document search. Every factual statement should carry a source ID in square brackets; the copilot gives no repair or disassembly procedures.

docs.title: What data is real and what is synthetic
docs.text: Real: the 3D scan of the equipment room. Synthetic: all asset data comes from the Valmet x Since AI builder pack, a synthetic 16-sheet workbook (Asset_Master, Current_State, Telemetry_Sample_3d, Alarms_Events, Maintenance_History, Historical_Service_Cases, Knowledge_Docs, Data_Quality and others); all 30 assets are classified SYNTHETIC and every record has a synthetic_record flag. Illustrative: the X-Ray teaching models, lessons and practice, the Value calculator and any example expert reply. Approximate: object labels, asset-to-object mapping, scale and the layout simulation. There is no live plant data, no historian and no CMMS connection.

docs.title: What Plan mode does
docs.text: Plan mode is a maintenance-planning simulation. The technician moves a virtual proxy of an object (in the demo, the hand pallet truck that blocks P-005's service area); the app checks collisions against object boxes and the occupancy grid, shows clearance from the distance transform and the service zone, and re-plans the robot route with the changed layout (in the demo 8.40 m to 7.98 m). The plan can be reset or exported. The scan itself is never changed. It is an approximate simulation, not an engineering clearance or installation check; the service-zone size is an assumed example.

docs.title: What Support mode does
docs.text: Support mode is an asynchronous remote-support hand-off. The technician pins notes on 3D locations, writes a question and shares a support package (link, code or file) that carries the pins, notes, plan, camera view and asset context. The expert opens it, adds pins and a recommendation (optionally starting from a cited AI draft that must be reviewed) and a draft work order, and sends a package back. There is no live multi-user session, no video and no connection to plant controls.

docs.title: X-Ray, Learn and Practice
docs.text: X-Ray shows an exploded teaching model of the selected asset's equipment type: process pump, electric motor, control valve, pressure transmitter or vibration sensor (49 components in total). Each component has its function, failure symptoms, evidence signals and fault codes, and a diagnosis highlights the suspect components. Learn gives guided lessons on the model; Practice is a scored exercise behind a safety check. The models are procedural and illustrative: not reconstructed from the scan, not OEM drawings, not a Valmet product, and the content is not certified training or a procedure for real equipment.

docs.title: Work-order drafts
docs.text: The copilot can draft a work order for an asset (inspection, priority from urgency, recommended check, evidence IDs, safety prerequisites: work permit, isolation and lockout/tagout, OEM or site-approved procedure, qualified personnel). It is only a draft that requires planner approval; it is never sent to a CMMS and it performs no control action.

docs.title: How it could connect to plant data (design only)
docs.text: Not built; a design note. Read-only adapters would replace the synthetic workbook without changing the copilot: OPC UA subscriptions and reads (never Write or Call) for current values and alarms; a historian read API for telemetry baselines; MQTT Sparkplug B subscriptions with the broker denying any publish to command topics; a CMMS or EAM read API for the asset register and work orders; a document-management read API for manuals. Each adapter maps external identifiers to asset IDs through a reviewed mapping table and attaches provenance (source, observed time, received time, synthetic, replayed or live). Stale or poor-quality data lowers confidence. There is no write path back into plant systems.

docs.title: What a pilot would measure
docs.text: None of these are measured in the prototype. A pilot would measure: object-identification precision and recall on a human-labelled random sample; the share of target assets located correctly in the scan; time to find a piece of equipment with and without the tool; time to prepare a maintenance visit; planning collisions or access problems caught before the visit; technician training performance; time to assemble a remote-support case and get an expert answer; start-up time and frame rate on standard laptops; technician confidence and usability ratings (for example SUS). It would also compare copilot suggestions with technician outcomes (agreement, false alarms) and use replayed real data before any live connection.

docs.title: What is in the library
docs.text: The library (book icon, or ask 'show me the relevant manual') searches every citable document: the builder pack's 8 knowledge documents (one core diagnostic context per equipment type, the field-safety guardrail DOC-FIELD-SAFETY, the evidence-grounded response contract DOC-RAG-GUIDE and the 3D mapping contract DOC-3D-MAPPING), 30 asset cards generated from Asset_Master and Current_State, 50 historical service cases, 49 component training notes for the illustrative X-Ray models (KB-XRAY IDs) and the product documentation of this prototype (DOC-APP IDs). No OEM manuals were supplied; the training notes are general knowledge, not manufacturer instructions. Every answer cites these IDs and a click on an ID opens the document.

docs.title: The Value page
docs.text: The Value page is a calculator with editable, clearly hypothetical inputs (technicians, look-ups per week, weeks, minutes before and after) and the formula shown. No savings are measured, and the app has not been benchmarked against Unity or any other tool.
